title: Level 3 – Global Nurse Professional
subtitle: Mental Health Care
intro: Compassionate Mental Health Care Program Outline Welcome to the highest level of the GNPS learning pathway. Global Nursing Professionals influence mental health outcomes beyond individual encounters. They lead recovery-oriented services, reduce restrictive practice, strengthen suicide prevention, mentor teams and advocate against stigma and inequity. This level develops advanced capability in mental health leadership, quality improvement, trauma-informed systems, digital mental health, workforce wellbeing, service-user partnership and global mental health. Throughout this level you will strengthen your ability to: Lead recovery-oriented and rights-based mental health services Strengthen systems for suicide and violence prevention Analyse restrictive-practice and safety data Design and evaluate quality-improvement initiatives Promote trauma-informed and culturally safe systems Support integrated physical and mental healthcare Use digital mental health technologies safely and ethically Mentor teams in therapeutic practice and clinical reasoning Contribute to global mental health equity and anti-stigma work Mental health harm often reflects fragmented care, stigma, coercive systems, poor transitions or failure to recognise physical illness. Global Nursing Professionals identify these connections and lead practical improvements that protect dignity, safety and recovery. By completing Level 3, you should be prepared to lead mental health quality and safety initiatives, use evidence and data to strengthen services, support colleagues and contribute to recovery-oriented care locally and globally.

content.text: Leadership in mental health means creating services where people are treated with dignity, hope and partnership. Global Nursing Professionals model recovery-oriented practice and ensure that organisational systems support rather than undermine these values.
Learning outcomes
Lead recovery-oriented mental health practice Promote service-user and family partnership
Support psychological safety and reflective practice Advocate for rights and anti-stigma action
Recovery Leadership Leaders ensure that care planning, language, routines and evaluation reflect personal goals, strengths and choice.
Co-production People with lived experience should participate in service design, education and evaluation as partners, not symbolic representatives.
Workforce Culture Reflective supervision, debriefing and psychological safety help staff manage complexity while maintaining compassion.
Rights and Stigma Leaders challenge discrimination, promote supported decision-making and ensure that mental illness does not reduce access to physical healthcare.

A service reviews its care plans with people who use the service and finds that goals are written mainly by clinicians. The team redesigns planning around the person's own recovery goals and measures participation at review meetings.
Key learning points
Align service systems with recovery values Include lived experience in meaningful decision-making
Support staff reflection and wellbeing Challenge stigma within and beyond healthcare

sections.title: Reducing Restrictive Practice and Strengthening Safety Systems

content.text: Restrictive practices can cause physical and psychological harm. Global Nursing Professionals analyse why restriction occurs and lead safer, trauma-informed alternatives while maintaining protection from serious risk.
Learning outcomes
Analyse restrictive-practice data Apply trauma-informed systems thinking
Strengthen suicide and violence prevention Evaluate safer alternatives
Restrictive-Practice Review Seclusion, restraint and forced treatment should be monitored by frequency, duration, population and context. Every event should prompt review and learning.
Trauma-Informed Systems Services should maximise safety, choice, collaboration and predictability while avoiding practices that recreate trauma.
Suicide Prevention Systems Reliable assessment, safety planning, follow-up after crisis and communication across transitions reduce risk.
Workplace and Environmental Safety Staffing, ward design, sensory environments, communication and access to meaningful activity influence behavioural escalation.

A unit has high restraint use during evening shifts. Review identifies crowding, limited activity, inconsistent staffing and delayed access to medication review. The service changes the environment and staffing pattern, introduces sensory support and monitors outcomes.
Key learning points
Look beyond individual behaviour to system conditions Use data to identify patterns and inequity
Prioritise prevention and early engagement Measure whether alternatives reduce harm

sections.title: Quality Improvement, Integrated Care and Population Mental Health

content.text: Mental health outcomes are shaped by service quality, physical health, housing, social connection, trauma and access to care. Improvement requires collaboration across traditional service boundaries.
Learning outcomes
Use mental health data to identify improvement priorities Apply structured quality-improvement methods
Promote integrated physical and mental healthcare Address equity and social determinants
Quality Priorities Possible priorities include suicide follow-up, physical-health monitoring, medication safety, restrictive practice, readmission and continuity of care.
Integrated Care Mental health, primary care, emergency, substance-use and social services should coordinate around the person rather than operate in isolation.
Measurement Outcome, process, experience and balancing measures show whether change is effective and acceptable.
Equity Data should be examined across culture, gender, age, disability, geography and socioeconomic conditions to identify unequal access or outcomes.

A community service identifies poor metabolic monitoring for people receiving antipsychotics. Nurses introduce a shared physical-health pathway, reminders, primary-care communication and peer-supported education. Completion rates and follow-up improve.
Key learning points
Define the problem with reliable data Include service-user experience in evaluation
Connect mental and physical healthcare Examine who benefits and who remains excluded

sections.title: Digital Mental Health and Global Collaboration

content.text: Digital platforms, telehealth, apps and predictive tools can expand mental health support, but they also create risks involving privacy, exclusion, misinformation and over-reliance on algorithms. Global professionals use technology critically and ethically.
Learning outcomes
Evaluate digital mental health technologies Protect privacy and therapeutic relationships
Recognise digital exclusion and algorithmic bias Contribute to global mental health learning
Tele-mental Health Virtual care can improve access but requires identity confirmation, privacy, emergency plans and awareness of what cannot be assessed remotely.
Apps and Online Support Digital tools should be evidence-informed, transparent and integrated with appropriate clinical support. They should not replace urgent assessment.
Data and Algorithms Predictive tools may support decision-making but can reflect biased data. Nurses must retain professional judgement and explain limitations.
Global Mental Health Collaboration should support accessible, culturally relevant and sustainable care while respecting local knowledge and resources.

A rural service introduces video mental health reviews. Leaders establish privacy guidance, crisis escalation pathways and telephone alternatives for people without internet access. Technology improves access without becoming the only route to care.
Key learning points
Technology supports but does not replace therapeutic judgement Plan for emergencies during remote care
Protect privacy and address digital exclusion Adapt global learning to local culture and resources

End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 8 - Level 3, you have developed the advanced perspective of a Global Nursing Professional. You are prepared not only to provide compassionate mental health care but also to lead recovery-oriented services, reduce restrictive practice, improve systems, support digital innovation and advocate for equitable mental wellbeing.
GNPS Learning Pathway Level 1 - Qualified Nurse: Build foundations in recovery, communication, assessment, common conditions and safety.
Level 2 - International Qualified Nurse: Manage complex risk, medication, law and culturally safe international practice.
Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional: Lead rights-based services, quality improvement, integrated care and global mental health innovation.
